                                     UFO Convention At Strange Integratron Building
  From: UFO UpDates - Toronto <ufoupdates.nul>
  Date: Sat, 29 Apr 2006 11:32:44 -0400
  Fwd Date: Sat, 29 Apr 2006 11:32:44 -0400
  Subject: UFO Convention At Strange Integratron Building



  Source: KLAS-TV - Las Vegas, Nevada
  http://www.klas-tv.com/Global/story.asp?S=4834694
  April 29, 2006

  UFO Convention At Strange Integratron Building
  George Knapp, Investigative Reporter

  One of the strangest buildings in the world will be the site of
  a retro UFO convention this weekend, a throwback to gatherings
  that once attracted 10,000 or more devotees to the desert.
  The building is known as the Integratron, and UFO's or not, it's
  unquestionably strange. The Eyewitness News I-Team's George
  Knapp just had to see the place.
  The weird humming coming from the spacey-looking building sounds
  like a UFO warming up its engine for a quick jaunt to reticulum.
  It wouldn't be out of place. For the past half century, the high
  desert area around Landers California has been a Mecca for E.T.
  believers and enlightenment seekers.
  In the early '50s, an aircraft mechanic named George Van Tassel
  says he received telepathic messages from space aliens that told
  him how to build the Integratron, part-healing chamber, part
  time machine.
  'The Integratron is an historical building that was originally
  meant to be a big electrostatic generator," said Nancy Karl,
  Integratron manager. Karl, who is a New Yorker, and her sister
  came out for a visit to the Integratron and were hooked. That
  was 18 years ago.
  Even if the design really wasn't supplied by E.T.'s, and even if
  there isn't an energy vortex here, people say there's something
  about the place. "It seems to focus and amplify. It just happens
  to be a very zappy place. People seem to pop through whatever
  seems to be happening for them," Karl said.
  Van Tassel died before finishing the Integratron so it's never
  really worked as he envisioned it. Nancy Karl says the bottom
  chamber was supposed to generate negative ions that would heal
  the tissues of anyone who walked through.
  No nails or screws were used to build the Integratron, which
  makes the place as resonant as the inside of a giant violin. The
  top chamber is acoustically perfect, Karl says, but can play
  games with your head.
  The Karl sisters offer visitors what they call a sound bath.
  They rub little sticks on the sides of pure crystal bowls and
  the sound that comes out feels like it passes right through your
  body.



http://www.ufoupdateslist.com/2006/apr/m29-017.shtml[10/12/2011 19:08:31]
UFO Convention At Strange Integratron Building

  Not surprisingly, the Integratron attracts a lot of artists,
  writers, and show biz people for soul searching or even
  corporate retreats. Whether or not it's really tapped into the
  cosmos, there are worse ways to spend a day.

UFOs Are Back




                                                          UFO Updates
                                   A mailing list for the study of UFO-related phenomena
                                               'Its All Here In Black & White'
    Location: UFOUpDatesList.Com > 2006 > Apr > Apr 29

                                                                UFOs Are Back
  From: Nick Pope <nick.nul>
  Date: Sat, 29 Apr 2006 09:10:03 +0100
  Fwd Date: Sat, 29 Apr 2006 11:38:08 -0400
  Subject: UFOs Are Back

  In response to recent 'ufology is dead' articles in the media,
  my agent asked me to write something for the publishing
  industry, setting the record straight.
  Here's the article:
  -----
  Source: The Andrew Lowney Literary Agency - London, UK
  http://www.andrewlownie.co.uk/articles/2006/april_07UFO.shtml
  April 2006 News Letter
  Nick Pope, former UFO desk officer at the MOD and author of
  several UFO books argues that interest in UFOs is returning.

  UFOs Are Back
  UFOs are back. After a period when interest in the subject had
  waned, the topic is suddenly generating a vast amount of media
  coverage. So what's going on and what are the implications for
  publishers and authors?
  First of all, I should declare an interest. I used to run the
  British Government's UFO Project at the Ministry of Defence.
  I've written four books on the subject, all of which were
  agented (can I use a noun as a verb if my editor isn't looking?)
  by Andrew Lownie.
  Interest in UFOs is cyclic. The last peak came in the mid-
  Nineties. In 1995, the so-called 'alien autopsy' film was
  released: grainy black and white footage that some said showed a
  vaguely humanoid extraterrestrial being cut open by US military
  surgeons. Believers claimed this was the proof they'd been
  waiting for, while sceptics said that the film was a clever
  hoax. 1997 saw the 50th anniversary of America's first 'flying
  saucer' sighting and of the Roswell incident, where something
  (alien spacecraft or weather balloon, depending on who you
  believe) crashed in the New Mexico desert. Publishers, the media
  and the public were intrigued by all this and numerous books
  appeared. They did well. Authors such as Timothy Good were on
  the bestseller lists and my own first effort 'Open Skies Closed
  Minds' got to number three in the hardback non-fiction list and
  stayed in the top ten for ten weeks.
  However, in publishing as in economics, every boom is followed
  by a bust. The market was saturated and the view was that
  publishers had overbought. Interest in UFOs fell away, replaced
  perhaps by an interest in magic. Flying saucers and aliens gave
  way to the fictional worlds of Harry Potter, Narnia and The Lord
  of the Rings. But now, things are changing. Perhaps driven by
  interest in Dan Brown's 'The Da Vinci Code', people are
  rediscovering their interest in real life mysteries.
  Interest in UFOs is rising quickly and steadily. This is being
  fuelled by the Freedom of Information Act - the MOD is being
  bombarded with requests for documents on UFOs, and a look at


http://www.ufoupdateslist.com/2006/apr/m29-018.shtml[10/12/2011 19:08:32]
UFOs Are Back

  their website confirms this is virtually the most popular type
  of request they receive. The media have been quick to recognise
  the resurgence of interest. Over the Christmas period several
  national newspapers ran major features on the 25th anniversary
  of Britain's most famous UFO sighting, the Rendlesham Forest
  incident. Ant & Dec's new movie 'Alien Autopsy' is a fictional
  retelling of the story that sparked so much interest in 1995.
  Various UFO-related documentaries are in pre-production. But the
  real clue is in the way the subject is spilling out into a wider
  arena. The Science Museum have been running an exhibition about
  alien life, and my own recent TV appearances include not just
  documentaries, but popular entertainment programmes such as 'The
  New Paul O'Grady Show' and 'Totally Doctor Who'.
  All the signs are there: the UFO is back. It remains to be seen
  how the publishing industry will respond, but I suspect the next
  few years will be an interesting time. Oh, and next year
  sees the 60th anniversary of the Roswell crash!
  Andrew Lownie writes a monthly newsletter, which includes details
  of the Agency's latest news as well as advice for authors.
  -----
  Best wishes,
  Nick Pope
  http://www.nickpope.net

  have quipped that he was far too young and lacking in knowledge

  upbringing - or about yours - but I do know that being a nuclear
  physicist is no reason whatever for supposing that someone is
  more qualified to speak about crashed saucers, cover-ups and

  >>One thing I think we can say in this case (and Jerry can

  >>thereto at that time, as can be said of the 1896-97 stories.
  >>One must always consider the possibility of newspaper hoaxes
  >>or jokes, especially at certain periods of history. But in
  >>1920?
  >I've searched for other information, so far to no avail. So,
  >unfortunately, we're stuck with a poorly written, thoroughly
  >inadequate story which is open to any number of
  >interpretations and speculations.
  >Somebody - I believe it was James Smith - suggested that the
  >pilot had survived the wreck and carried off the motor,
  >presumably under his own power. A reasonable guess, perhaps,
  >but for me the problem - not necessarily an insurmountable one
  >- is that it presumes that (1) the guy was uninjured and (2)

  >in the dark.
  Very true, Jerry.
  In another post I explained the implausibility of the pilot
  packing out the engine due to its considerable weight.
  The weight to horsepower ratios 2.3:1 of engines in 1915 to 1920
  was greater than today's 1935 - yes 1935 & they haven't improved
  much - technology recip. engines used on most present day,
  light, factory-built aircraft. In the case of any possible small
  aircraft in this scenario, the engine would have run from 80-150
  horsepower - at full RPM - with weights of 180 to 350 pounds.
  Carrying it any appreciable distance would have involved at
  least two men, possible three, and a travois or a small cart,
  then a vehicle of some sort once a road was reached. I've had
  occasion to lift these engines - with other helper and on a nice
  smooth hangar floor - while attaching them to their motor mounts
  and they are extremely heavy and cumbersome.

                                                                  A Short Story
  From: UFO UpDates - Toronto <ufoupdates.nul>
  Date: Sun, 30 Apr 2006 09:53:51 -0400
  Fwd Date: Sun, 30 Apr 2006 09:53:51 -0400
  Subject: A Short Story



  This from 'The Norm'
  ebk
  -----
  A Short Story
  On a remote island in the Pacific ocean there is a society of
  people who have been quite isolated from the industrialized
  world. Although relatively technologically primitive, by our
  standards, the people of this society are socially and morally
  advanced.
  For many years, there has been a major emotional controversy
  among the inhabitants of this island regarding whether so-called
  "man-made airplanes" actually exist. There have been alleged
  visual sightings of "airplanes" high in the sky by some
  residents of the island, but these reported sightings have
  usually been denied and ignored by most of the other island
  residents. The witnesses of "airplane sightings" have often been
  ridiculed by politicians and other powerful members of the
  society.
  However, during an important meeting of the island residents, a
  well-known and respected former statesman of this society gave
  an unprecedented speech in which he emphatically proclaimed to
  his astonished audience:
  "You must believe me. Man-made airplanes do exist. They are as
  real as the UFOs that fly over our heads!"
  -----

  was generally accepted. Of course, such explanations are not
  certain, in the scientific sense, as modern science is based on
  probability rather than certainty. However, some UFO
  explanations are rather more probable than others.

  A general comment. There seem to be two arguments being forth in
  various editorials.
  One argument being put forth is that 'ufology is dead' in the
  sense that there are fewer books on this subject being published
  by publishers now than in former boom times. That could well be
  true, but unless you are an author trying to get published it
  doesn't seem like much of a concern. Publishing houses work in
  cycles, as Nick says, or perhaps everything that could be said
  about our current understanding of these encounters has been
  said - and until some authors realize a new level of insight,
  there won't be much interest from publishers.
  Of more relevance to those interested in the study of alien
  encounters is the other argument being put forth -- that
  'ufology is dead' because there are fewer ufo sightings or alien
  encounters being reported in recent years.
  In a 2005 article headlined "Pine Bush outgrows UFOs" (Times
  Herald-Record, Steve Israel, 9 December 2005), the paper asks
  "Pine Bush - Where have all the UFOs gone? Check out the list of
  sightings on the menu of the Cup and (Flying) Saucer diner. The
  list stops in 1999."
  But that newspaper's story came four years after people in the
  midst of alien encounter research noticed the same thing:
  "What's really interesting [is] two years ago all these close
  encounters abruptly ended," Whitley Strieber told the University
  of Colorado student newspaper in 2001 - referring not to own
  experiences, but rather to experiences among people in general.
  (He has said that his own contact experiences essentially ended
  when he left upstate New York in late 1997).
  At the John Mack Institute, in the 2003 documentary film
  "Touched" by Laurel Chiten (filmed between late 2000 and early
  2003), experiencers who John Mack had worked with who'd had
  recurrent experiences throughout their lives reported that
  visits from the apparent aliens had changed, becoming infrequent
  or entirely absent.
  Has there been a change? Seems so. And if so, 'What does it

  mean?' is a more relevant question than 'is ufology dead?'.
